passage: he found himself transformed in his bed into a horrible vermin
text:
Gregor Samsa wakes to find he has become a monstrous insect-like creature in his bed.

The selected line is the opening of Kafka's story, which begins with the transformation already accomplished. Gregor wakes from troubled dreams and finds himself changed into a "horrible vermin" p. 1. The vermin is never named as a specific species, and the text describes it through its armour-like back, brown domed belly, and many pitifully thin legs p. 1.

The phrase matters because the story treats the change as a fact to be lived with rather than explained. Gregor first wonders whether it is a dream and concludes that it is not p. 1. His concern moves quickly to his job as a travelling salesman and his family's debts, which the rest of the story keeps returning to.

question: How does Grete change over the three parts?
What happens to the family after Gregor dies?
text:
Grete begins as a gentle, anxious sister. In Part I she pleads at his door, "Gregor, open the door, I beg of you" p. 5. In Part II she becomes his caretaker. She tests his tastes with a whole selection of food, leaves the room so he can eat unwatched p. 27, and takes over the heavy work. Yet she cannot hide her revulsion: she throws the window open as if suffocating p. 35. Her confidence grows, and she insists on clearing all his furniture, which the narrator links to her new assurance p. 40. She speaks to him directly for the first time only when he is on the wall, with a shaken fist p. 43.

By Part III she works in a shop and studies shorthand and French p. 48, and she grows careless with his room, though she is jealously possessive of cleaning it p. 52. After the tenants' departure she turns on him: "I don't want to call this monster my brother... we have to try and get rid of it" p. 61. She insists "You've got to get rid of the idea that that's Gregor" p. 63, and she locks him in with "At last!" p. 65.

After his death, the family responds with relief. Mr. Samsa says, "let's give thanks to God for that" p. 66. He throws out the three tenants p. 68. They write excuse letters and take a day's outing by tram p. 69. On the ride they find their jobs are good and their prospects not bad, and they plan a smaller, cheaper flat p. 70. The parents notice that Grete is blossoming and think it will soon be time to find her a husband. The story ends with Grete stretching her young body p. 71.

question: Who are the three gentlemen and why do they leave?
text:
The three gentlemen are lodgers. The family rents out one of the flat's rooms to them because money is short p. 54. All three have full beards and are painfully insistent on tidiness, in their own room and throughout the flat, especially the kitchen. They bring most of their own furnishings, which pushes the family's surplus belongings into Gregor's room p. 54. The middle gentleman acts as their authority, tasting the meat first p. 56. The document gives no names or backgrounds for them.

They leave in two stages. First, Grete plays the violin in the living room at their invitation, and Gregor crawls out toward her, covered in dust p. 58. The middle gentleman points him out, and the men realize they have had a neighbour like Gregor without knowing it. He then gives immediate notice, refuses to pay for the days he has stayed, and threatens an action for damages, citing "the repugnant conditions that prevail in this flat" p. 61. The other two join in.

Second, after Gregor dies, they come out expecting breakfast. Mr. Samsa orders them out: "Leave my home. Now!" p. 67. They are cowed and go, bowing silently p. 68. So they had already given notice, but the family expels them anyway.

Part I

Gregor Samsa wakes to find himself transformed into a huge insect, and tries to get out of bed and face his family and his employer's chief clerk. The part sets up the household, his debts and the fear for his job.

Where we are

A morning in the Samsa flat, shortly before seven. Gregor, a travelling salesman, is late for his five o'clock train and lies in his locked bedroom. p. 3
He supports his parents and sister and must work off his parents' debt to his boss, so missing work threatens the whole family's security. p. 3
The chief clerk arrives from the firm to investigate his absence, while family members call through the three doors of his room. p. 9

People

Gregor Samsa — The travelling salesman who wakes transformed, anxious about work and his family, and still thinking in human terms.
Mother — Gentle, asthmatic, and defends Gregor to the chief clerk as hardworking and unwell.
Father — Gregor's father, who calls through the door and later takes charge when the crisis breaks.
Grete — Gregor's sister, who speaks to him through the side door and begs him to open it.
The chief clerk — The firm's senior representative, who is suspicious, scolds Gregor and hints that his position is insecure.

Threads to watch

Gregor's job and the family debt: the chief clerk questions his sales and hints at missing money, so the threat to his position grows. p. 12
Communication: Gregor's voice has changed, and he cannot tell whether he can still be understood by those outside his door. p. 4
How the family and the chief clerk will react once they see Gregor, and whether he can control his new body. p. 15
